# SK1031 — Use a null-conditional assignment

<!-- Generated from Rules/Rikarin.Skala.Rules.Metadata/rules.json. Do not edit. -->

An `if` whose only job is to null-check the receiver of one assignment is `?.` in C# 14.

| | |
|---|---|
| Category | Modernization |
| Default severity | suggestion |
| Scope | Semantic |
| Needs a compilation | yes |
| Fix | yes, safe |
| Language version floor | 14.0 |
| Since | 1.2 |

## Why

C# 14 allows a null-conditional expression on the left of an assignment, so the three-line guard around a single field or property write becomes one line that says the same thing. The rewrite is exact rather than nearly exact because the feature evaluates the right-hand side only when the receiver is non-null, which is what the `if` did.

## Example

Instead of:

```csharp
if (customer is not null) {
    customer.Order = order;
}
```

Write:

```csharp
customer?.Order = order;
```

## When it does not fire

None known. The receiver must be a chain of plain names, since the original evaluates it twice and `?.` evaluates it once. The tested expression must be the exact link of the target's chain that was guarded: `if (a.B is not null) a.B.C = v;` rewritten as `a?.B.C = v` would reinstate the NullReferenceException the guard existed to prevent, so the `?` goes where the test was. `x != null` is admitted only where the operand's type declares no `operator ==`, the same proof SK1010 makes. It is silent on an `if` with an `else`, on a body that is not exactly one simple assignment, on a compound assignment, on a receiver that is not a reference type, and inside an expression tree.
